# Observability for Agents {#sec-observability}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Chapter status: drafted.** One small measurement: five agent runs
instrumented with spans shaped by the OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions, to find
out what a trace actually costs in spans and bytes. The convention details are
read off the specification rather than recalled — it moved repositories in 2026
and most of it is still unstable, which is itself something to plan around.
Software: `ollama` 0.24.0 serving `llama3.2:3b`, Python 3.14.5, Apple Silicon;
conventions read from `open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai` at
2026-08-27.
:::

**Learning objectives.** After this chapter you can:

- say which parts of an agent trace are ordinary distributed tracing and which
  three parts genuinely differ;
- instrument with the GenAI conventions, and know how much of them is settled
  enough to depend on;
- read a trace hierarchy from session down to a single tool call;
- estimate what your telemetry will cost in spans and bytes before you turn it
  on;
- attribute token spend to a user, a team and a feature;
- go from a user complaint to the failing span as a repeatable procedure;
- say what tracing does not cover, and where that work belongs instead.

## An agent trace is a distributed trace, with three differences {#sec-observability-same}

The good news first, because it saves a lot of reinvention. An agent run is a
tree of nested operations with parents, children, timings and errors — which is
exactly what distributed tracing was built for. Spans, trace context
propagation, sampling, exporters and every backend you already run apply
unchanged.

Three things genuinely differ, and they are where the GenAI conventions earn
their existence:

**The interesting payload is text, and it is large.** An HTTP span records a
method and a status. An LLM span's most useful content is the prompt and the
completion, which are kilobytes and which contain whatever the user typed.
@sec-observability-cost measures what that does to volume, and
@sec-observability-privacy deals with what it does to your obligations.

**Cost is an attribute, not an afterthought.** Ordinary spans have a duration.
LLM spans also have input and output token counts, and those convert to money.
That makes a trace the natural place to answer "what did this feature cost?",
which is a question tracing systems were not previously asked.

**Failure is often not an error.** A span with `status=OK` can contain a
confidently wrong answer, a hallucinated tool argument, or an agent that hit
its step ceiling and stopped. @sec-deployment made hitting a ceiling a
first-class outcome for exactly this reason: nothing in the transport layer
knows the run failed.

## The conventions, and how much of them is settled {#sec-observability-semconv}

Instrumenting with your own attribute names works until you want a vendor's UI,
a shared dashboard, or a migration. The OpenTelemetry **GenAI semantic
conventions** are the agreed vocabulary, and two facts about their current state
matter more than any individual attribute name.

**They moved.** As of 2026 the GenAI conventions live in their own repository,
`open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai`, split out of the main
`semantic-conventions` repo — where the old paths now carry nothing but a
forwarding notice. Documentation, blog posts and instrumentation libraries
written before the split point at pages that no longer hold the spec.

**Most of them are not stable.** Counting the stability badges — one per marked
item, which is not the same as one per distinct attribute, since an attribute
can be marked in more than one document — in the span, agent-span and metric
documents of the repository snapshot counted for this chapter in 2026 (the
commit was not recorded, so expect later versions to differ): **286 of 308 marked items in the span conventions are
`Development`, and only 22 are `Stable`** — with much the same
ratio in the agent and metric documents. At that snapshot the new repository
had no tagged release.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
[A convention marked `Development` can change its attribute names between
versions, and roughly nine in ten of these are.]{.hl} That is not a reason to
avoid them — they are still the only common vocabulary — but it is a reason to
pin the version you instrumented against, to record it, and to expect a
migration rather than to be surprised by one.
:::

With that stated, the shape is stable enough to teach. Span names are formulaic
rather than free text:

| operation | span name | example |
|:--|:--|:--|
| a model call | `{gen_ai.operation.name} {gen_ai.request.model}` | `chat llama3.2:3b` |
| a tool call | `execute_tool {gen_ai.tool.name}` | `execute_tool lookup` |
| a retrieval | `{gen_ai.operation.name} {gen_ai.data_source.id}` | `retrieval kb-main` — use the retrieval operation for the search itself and keep `embeddings` for the call that produced the vectors; they are two spans, not one |
| an agent turn | `{gen_ai.operation.name}` | `invoke_agent` |

: Span naming, as the specification defines it {tbl-colwidths="[20,42,38]"}

The operation names are an **open** enum with a well-known list — the
specification's own wording is that if one of the listed values applies you
MUST use it, and otherwise you MAY define your own — and reading that list
tells you what the working group thinks an agent *is*: `chat`,
`text_completion`, `generate_content`, `embeddings`, `retrieval`,
`execute_tool`, `plan`, `invoke_agent`, `create_agent`, `invoke_workflow`,
`fetch_response`, plus a family of memory operations. A planning phase, a
retrieval operation distinct from embedding, and memory CRUD arriving in a
tracing spec is a fair summary of where @sec-memory, @sec-rag and
@sec-deployment ended up. The list grows; check it rather than copying this
one.

The attributes worth knowing by heart are few, out of 65 in the span document
alone:

```text
gen_ai.operation.name        chat, execute_tool, invoke_agent, ...
gen_ai.provider.name         who served it
gen_ai.request.model         what you asked for
gen_ai.response.model        what answered — not always the same
gen_ai.usage.input_tokens    the cost that dominates (chapter 31)
gen_ai.usage.output_tokens
gen_ai.conversation.id       what stitches a session together
gen_ai.agent.name            which agent, when you have several
gen_ai.tool.name             which tool
gen_ai.input.messages        the prompt — see "Sensitive data in telemetry"
gen_ai.output.messages       the completion
```

Two of those repay attention. `gen_ai.response.model` differs from
`gen_ai.request.model` whenever an alias resolves to a dated version — which is
@sec-gateway's pinning problem, visible in your traces if you record both and
invisible if you record one. And `gen_ai.conversation.id` is what turns a pile
of spans into a session you can replay.

The metrics are similarly formulaic, and one of them should look familiar:

```text
gen_ai.client.token.usage             tokens, by type
gen_ai.client.operation.duration      end-to-end per call
gen_ai.server.time_to_first_token     chapter 31's TTFT, as a metric
gen_ai.server.time_per_output_token   the decode rate, as a metric
gen_ai.execute_tool.duration
gen_ai.invoke_agent.duration
```

[The serving measurements from @sec-serving are not a separate exercise; they
are two of the standard metrics.]{.hl} If you instrument to the convention you
get something close to the prefill/decode split as a dashboard rather than as a
one-off experiment. Close, not identical: measured from the client, TTFT also
contains queueing at the server and the first decode step, so it is prefill plus
whatever the request waited for. Watch the two together and remember that a
rising TTFT can mean a longer prompt or a busier server, and only a server-side
breakdown separates them.

## The hierarchy, and where to hang each id {#sec-observability-hierarchy}

A trace is only navigable if the levels are consistent. Five, and the mistake
teams make is collapsing the middle two:

:::: {.anlp-fig}
```{=html}
<div class="fig-title">One agent run, as spans</div>
<svg viewBox="0 0 760 268" role="img" aria-label="Nested span diagram for a single agent run, showing session, run, agent, model call and tool call levels">
  <text x="8" y="18" class="t-xs t-muted t-b">SESSION &#183; gen_ai.conversation.id &#183; many runs, one user</text>
  <rect x="8" y="26" width="744" height="32" rx="6" class="box"/>
  <text x="20" y="47" class="t-sm t-mono">conv-042</text>
  <text x="736" y="47" class="t-xs t-muted t-end">days</text>

  <rect x="28" y="88" width="704" height="32" rx="6" class="box"/>
  <text x="40" y="109" class="t-sm t-mono">invoke_agent maintenance-bot</text>
  <text x="716" y="109" class="t-xs t-muted t-end">2.6 s</text>

  <text x="48" y="142" class="t-xs t-accent t-b">STEPS &#183; alternating model call and tool call</text>

  <rect x="48"  y="150" width="150" height="30" rx="5" class="box-accent"/>
  <text x="58"  y="170" class="t-xs t-mono">chat llama3.2:3b</text>
  <rect x="206" y="150" width="118" height="30" rx="5" class="box"/>

  <rect x="490" y="150" width="118" height="30" rx="5" class="box"/>
  <text x="500" y="170" class="t-xs t-mono">execute_tool</text>
  <rect x="616" y="150" width="116" height="30" rx="5" class="box-accent"/>
  <text x="626" y="170" class="t-xs t-mono">chat</text>

  <path d="M8,200 H752" class="ln-thin"/>
  <text x="8"   y="222" class="t-xs t-muted t-b">ON THE MODEL SPANS</text>
  <text x="8"   y="240" class="t-xs t-mono">usage.input_tokens &#183; usage.output_tokens &#183; response.model</text>
  <text x="8"   y="256" class="t-xs t-muted">cost lives here, and rolls up to every level above</text>
  <text x="440" y="222" class="t-xs t-muted t-b">ON THE TOOL SPANS</text>
  <text x="440" y="240" class="t-xs t-mono">tool.name &#183; call.arguments &#183; call.result</text>

</svg>
```

::: {.fig-cap}
Five levels, and the two ids that make them navigable: a conversation id that
survives across runs, and a trace id per run. Token counts sit on the model
spans and roll up; everything above them is arithmetic. The measured run here
averaged 4.8 spans — one agent span, 2.4 model calls and 1.4 tool calls.
:::
::::

The two collapses to avoid: putting every run in one trace, which makes a
week-long conversation a single unnavigable tree; and giving each step its own
trace, which loses the run. **One trace per run, one conversation id across
runs** is the shape that supports both "show me this request" and "show me this
user's week".

## What a trace costs {#sec-observability-cost}

Instrumentation is usually adopted without an estimate, and the bill arrives
later. Five agent runs, spans shaped as above:

```text
 task  spans  chat  tool    bytes  w/o content
    1      4     2     1     2467         1363
    2      6     3     2     4059         2029
    3      6     3     2     4260         2032
    4      4     2     1     2489         1370
    5      4     2     1     2562         1388

spans per run        4.8
bytes per run        3,167
  without content    1,636
content share        48.3%
```

Half the volume is the prompt and completion text — and [these are toy prompts:
content was 48.3% in this sample, and its share rises in the projection below as
soon as only the prompt grows]{.hl}. The runs above averaged 301 prompt
tokens. @sec-summarization measured a realistic single-shot request at **890
prompt tokens**, and @sec-serving worked with contexts of 4,258. Holding the
measured structure fixed at 1,636 bytes per run and scaling the measured 1,531
bytes of content linearly in prompt size:

| prompt size per call | bytes per run | content share | against structure alone |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| 301 tokens (measured here) | 3,167 | 48.3% | 1.9× |
| 890 tokens (@sec-summarization) | 6,163 | 73.4% | 3.8× |
| 4,258 tokens (@sec-serving) | 23,294 | 93.0% | 14.2× |

: Trace volume against prompt size, structure held fixed
{tbl-colwidths="[34,22,22,22]"}

At a million runs a month that is 4.8M spans and **1.6 GB of structure against
6.2 GB with realistic prompts recorded** — a near-fourfold difference that is
entirely the decision to log content, and a fourteen-fold one at long context.

So the decision to record prompts is a storage decision, a retention decision
and a privacy decision at the same time, and it should be made deliberately
rather than by leaving a default on. The usual resolution is to sample:
structure on every run, content on a small percentage and on every error.

## Attributing cost {#sec-observability-attribution}

Token counts on model spans are what make @sec-governance's unit economics
possible, and the mechanism is unglamorous: put the dimensions you will want to
group by on the span, because you cannot add them retrospectively.

The four that are almost always wanted, and none of which are in the GenAI
conventions because they are yours rather than the model's: user id, team or
tenant, feature, and environment.

**Attaching them is not as simple as it sounds, and the obvious way does not
work.** Span attributes are *not* inherited in OpenTelemetry: writing `user.id`
on the root span does not put it on any child, and nothing in the SDK or the
protocol propagates it. What propagates with the context is **Baggage**. So set
the keys in baggage at the root, and install a span processor that copies those
baggage keys onto every span it sees — `BaggageSpanProcessor` in the
`opentelemetry-python` contrib packages does exactly this. Environment is the
exception: it belongs on the **Resource**, which *is* attached to every span
the SDK emits. Some backends roll attributes up to the trace level and give the
impression that inheritance happened; that is a backend feature, not the
specification.

[The number worth reporting is not spend, it is spend per unit of value.]{.hl}
Cost per session flatters a feature nobody finishes; @sec-agent-eval made the
same argument for cost per *correct* answer. Cost per resolved ticket, per
completed task, per accepted suggestion — those are the numbers that survive a
budget review, and computing them needs the outcome on the trace too.

## From a complaint to the failing span {#sec-observability-rootcause}

The point of tracing is that debugging becomes a procedure rather than an
inspiration. A workable one:

1. **Find the session.** From a user report, `gen_ai.conversation.id` — which
   is why the id must reach your support tooling and not only your dashboard.
2. **Find the run.** One trace per run, ordered by time. If the complaint is
   "it was wrong", the run is the one before the complaint.
3. **Read the tool spans first, not the model spans.** What the agent *did* is
   in `gen_ai.tool.name` and its arguments, and it is far quicker to scan than
   the prompts.
4. **Find the first step where the trajectory diverges.** @sec-agent-eval's
   distinction applies here: the wrong answer is usually several steps after
   the wrong decision.
5. **Only then read that span's prompt and completion.** If you sampled content
   away, this is the step that fails — which is the argument for keeping content
   on errors.
6. **Turn it into a test.** @sec-agent-eval's regression discipline: the trace
   you just read is a scenario.

## What OpenTelemetry does not cover {#sec-observability-not}

Worth stating plainly, because vendors blur it. Tracing records **what
happened**: which model, how long, how many tokens, which tools, what errors.
It has nothing to say about whether the output was any good.

Faithfulness, accuracy, safety and quality are the evaluation layer —
@sec-llm-eval, @sec-agent-eval and @sec-production-eval — and they attach *to*
traces rather than being produced by them. A judge score can be recorded as a
span attribute; it is not something the tracing SDK knows.

The practical consequence is that "we have observability" and "we know whether
it works" are different claims, and a dashboard full of green spans is
compatible with a product that is confidently wrong on a third of requests.

## Sensitive data in telemetry {#sec-observability-privacy}

Prompts contain whatever users type, which in a support product is names,
addresses, order numbers and occasionally card details. Recording
`gen_ai.input.messages` therefore copies personal data into a system that was
designed for latency histograms.

Three consequences that follow, and they are engineering work rather than
policy statements:

**Redact at the boundary, before export.** A span processor that scrubs before
the exporter is the only place it can be done once. Redacting in the backend
means it was transmitted; redacting per instrumentation means five
implementations, which is @sec-gateway's argument in a different building.

**Telemetry has residency and retention obligations too.** The data is a copy of
the same personal data your database holds, and the fact that it lives in a
monitoring vendor does not exempt it. @sec-governance is where the obligations
themselves live.

**Sampling content is a privacy control, not only a cost one.** The measurement
above frames it as storage; it is also the difference between holding every
user's text and holding a small sample. Those happen to be the same decision,
which is convenient, and it is worth making it for both reasons at once.

## Intuition checks {#sec-observability-intuition}

Answer each one before you open it. The first and third are about what tracing
is and is not — the two claims most often conflated when this layer is bought
rather than built — and the rest carry the chapter's numbers: the content share
of a trace, the stability ratio in the conventions, and the two attributes that
make a silent model upgrade visible.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. You already run distributed tracing. What actually changes?

Less than vendors imply, and three things genuinely.

The payload is text and it is large, so volume is dominated by prompts rather
than by span count. Cost is an attribute rather than an afterthought, because
token counts convert to money and roll up. And failure is often not an error:
a span with `status=OK` can hold a confidently wrong answer or a run that hit
its step ceiling.

Everything else — context propagation, sampling, exporters, your backend — is
what you already have.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. Should you record prompts and completions?

It is a storage decision, a retention decision and a privacy decision at once,
so make it once, deliberately.

Measured here, content was 48.3% of trace volume on toy prompts of 301 tokens.
Scaling that content linearly to @sec-summarization's realistic 890 tokens puts
it at 73.4%, and at @sec-serving's long contexts 93.0% — a four- to
fourteen-fold difference in bytes that is entirely this one setting.

The usual resolution is to sample: structure on every run, content on a small
percentage and on every error. That keeps debugging possible where it matters
and stops you holding every user's text.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. Your dashboard is green and users say the agent is wrong. Contradiction?

No — you are reading the wrong instrument.

Tracing records what happened: models, durations, tokens, tools, exceptions. It
does not know whether the answer was any good, and a run that returns a fluent
falsehood in 900 ms is a healthy span by every transport-layer measure.

Quality lives in the evaluation layer (@sec-llm-eval, @sec-agent-eval,
@sec-production-eval) and attaches *to* traces as scores. "We have
observability" and "we know whether it works" are different claims.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 4. Why record both the requested and the responded model?

Because they differ exactly when it matters.

`gen_ai.request.model` is what you asked for; `gen_ai.response.model` is what
answered. When an unversioned alias resolves to a dated version — @sec-gateway's
silent-upgrade problem — the second changes and the first does not. Record both
and the upgrade appears in your traces on the day it happens; record one and you
find out from an output-quality regression weeks later.

It is two attributes and it converts an invisible dependency change into a
visible one.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 5. You instrumented to the GenAI conventions last year and names have changed.

Expected, and the fix is to have recorded which version you targeted.

The conventions moved repository in 2026 — into
`open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai` — and of the marked items in the
span document as counted here, 286 are `Development` against 22 `Stable`. At
that snapshot the new repository had no tagged release.

That is not an argument against using them; they remain the only common
vocabulary, and a vendor UI that understands them is worth a lot. It is an
argument for pinning, for recording the pin next to the instrumentation, and
for budgeting a migration rather than being surprised by one.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 6. Which cost number should a budget review see?

Cost per unit of value, not cost per session.

Cost per session flatters a feature nobody completes and punishes one that does
real work in several steps. @sec-agent-eval made the same argument for
evaluation with cost per *correct* answer; here it is cost per resolved ticket,
per completed task, per accepted suggestion.

Computing it means the outcome has to be on the trace, which is a two-line
change at the root span. Add it before you need it: you cannot group by a
dimension you did not record, and recovering it afterwards means joining traces
to some other system on a shared id — possible when that id was recorded, and a
data-engineering project rather than a dashboard filter.
:::

## Interview questions {#sec-observability-interview}

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**On sourcing — the same caveat as @sec-text-as-data.** The questions below
recur in the two credible open sources this book uses throughout, plus the ones
this chapter's own measurement makes answerable.
:::

### Testing whether you understand the layer

**Q: How is tracing an LLM agent different from tracing a microservice?**

Structurally it is not — spans, parents, context propagation and your existing
backend all apply. Three things differ: the payload is text and dominates
volume, so the interesting attribute is kilobytes rather than a status code;
cost is an attribute, because token counts convert to money and roll up the
tree; and a successful span can contain a wrong answer, so `status=OK` is not
evidence the run worked.

**Q: What would you put on an LLM span?**

Operation name, provider, requested *and* responded model, both token counts, a
conversation id, and your own dimensions — user, team, feature, environment —
because you cannot group by what you did not record. Then say what you would
sample rather than always record: the prompt and completion, which is most of
the volume.

**Q: How much telemetry will this generate?**

Answer with a method, not a number. Spans per run times traffic, plus bytes per
run — and note that bytes are dominated by prompts. Measured here at 4.8 spans
and 3.2 KB per run on toy prompts. Projected at @sec-summarization's realistic
890-token prompts the same structure is 6.2 KB, and content becomes 73.4% of it;
at 4,258-token contexts it is 23.3 KB and 93.0%. So the estimate turns almost
entirely on whether you record content.

### Testing whether you have shipped one

**Q: A user says the agent gave a wrong answer yesterday. Walk me through it.**

Conversation id from the support ticket — which means that id has to reach
support tooling, not just the dashboard. Then the run before the complaint, then
the tool spans before the model spans, because what the agent *did* is faster to
scan than what it read. Find the first step where the trajectory diverges, since
the wrong answer is usually several steps after the wrong decision. Then read
that span's prompt. Then turn it into a regression test.

**Q: Your monitoring bill tripled after adding LLM tracing. Why?**

Almost certainly content. Structure is small and roughly fixed per run; prompts
are not, and they grow with context. Projected from this chapter's measurement,
moving from 301-token prompts to 4,258-token ones takes a run from 3.2 KB to
23.3 KB with the same number of spans. The fix is sampling content while keeping structure on
everything, and keeping content on errors.

**Q: How do you keep personal data out of your traces?**

Redact before export, in a span processor, so it happens once for every
instrumentation rather than five times differently. Then say the two things
people miss: telemetry inherits the same residency and retention obligations as
the database, because it is a copy of the same data; and content sampling is a
privacy control as well as a cost one, which makes it an easy decision to
justify twice.

## Lab: instrument an agent, then debug it from the trace alone {#sec-observability-lab}

### Step 1 — instrument one agent to the convention

Model spans and tool spans, named as the specification says, carrying
`gen_ai.operation.name`, the request and response model, both token counts, and
a conversation id. Record which version of the conventions you instrumented
against — you will want it when the attribute names move.

### Step 2 — measure your own trace volume

Run twenty realistic requests and record spans per run, bytes per run, and bytes
with content stripped. Multiply by your monthly traffic. Do this *before*
turning on content recording, so the number informs the decision instead of
explaining the bill.

### Step 3 — add your own dimensions

User, team, feature, environment. Put the first three in baggage at the root,
install a baggage span processor, and confirm they appear on every child span —
if they do not, the processor is missing, because span attributes do not
propagate on their own. Environment goes on the Resource.

Then check where that baggage goes. Baggage travels in an HTTP header on every
outbound call the context reaches, including calls to your model provider and to
third-party tools, so a user id in baggage is a user id you are sending to them.
Redacting spans before export does not close that path — it is a different
channel. Configure the propagator so baggage is not injected on external calls,
or keep anything identifying out of baggage and attach it with a span processor
instead. Then produce cost per feature for a day.

### Step 4 — produce cost per unit of value

Add the outcome — resolved, abandoned, escalated — to the root span, and
recompute cost per *resolved* task. Compare the two rankings. If a feature
changes place, that is the point of the step.

### Step 5 — inject a fault and find it blind

Have somebody else break something: a tool returning stale data, a step ceiling
lowered, a prompt truncated. Then find it using only the trace, timing yourself.
Write down what you wished you had instrumented — that list is the real output
of this lab.

### Step 6 — redact, and prove it

Add a span processor that scrubs personal data before export. Send a request
containing an email address and a phone number, then search your backend for
both. Finding either is a failed step, not a finding.

### What to hand in

Your spans-per-run and bytes-per-run with and without content, projected to your
traffic; a cost-per-resolved-task table by feature; the time it took to find the
injected fault and the instrumentation you wished you had; and evidence that
redaction happens before export.

## Exercises {#sec-observability-exercises}

1. **Volume before the bill.** Instrument one workload, measure spans and bytes
   per run with and without content, and project to monthly traffic. Then decide
   your content sampling rate and write down the reasoning.

2. **Find the alias.** Record `gen_ai.request.model` and
   `gen_ai.response.model` for a week against a hosted provider. Report whether
   they ever diverged, and what you would have noticed if they had.

3. **Cost per resolved task.** Produce two rankings of your features — by cost
   per session and by cost per resolved task. Explain any feature that changes
   place.

4. **Blind debugging, timed.** Have a colleague inject a fault. Find it using
   only the trace and record the time. Repeat after adding the instrumentation
   you wished you had, and compare.

5. **The redaction test.** Send a request containing an email address and a
   phone number through your instrumented path, then search your telemetry
   backend for both. If either is present, your redaction is in the wrong place.

6. **Conventions drift.** Take an instrumentation library you use and find which
   version of the GenAI conventions it targets. Diff its attribute names against
   the current specification and list what would break.

7. **Sampling that keeps errors.** Implement content sampling that records 5% of
   successful runs and 100% of failures. Verify on real traffic that no failed
   run lost its prompt.

## Where to go deeper {#sec-observability-deeper}

Before reading: open one trace from a system you run and try to answer "what did
this request cost?" from it alone. Whether you can is the whole subject of this
chapter.

This chapter cites no papers, so there is one table rather than the usual two.
The specification is the primary source here, and it is a moving one — check the
stability badges yourself rather than trusting the ratio quoted above, which was
counted on a specific day.

| resource | what it is |
|:--|:--|
| [`semantic-conventions-genai`](https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai) | the specification itself, in its current home; read the stability badges before depending on any attribute name |
| [OpenTelemetry tracing concepts](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/traces/) | spans, context propagation and the model everything above assumes you already have |
| [The trace SDK specification](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/otel/trace/sdk/) | where span processors are defined — the hook redaction has to use to happen before export |
| [Sampling](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/sampling/) | head and tail sampling as the spec defines them; tail sampling is what lets you keep content on errors only |
| [`opentelemetry-python`](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-python) | the SDK, and the place to read what a span processor actually looks like |
| [`openinference`](https://github.com/Arize-ai/openinference) | instrumentation for the common agent frameworks, when you would rather not write spans by hand |
| [`arize-phoenix`](https://github.com/Arize-ai/phoenix) | a trace UI you can run locally; the cheapest way to learn what you wish you had recorded |
| [`langfuse`](https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse) / [`openllmetry`](https://github.com/traceloop/openllmetry) | two takes on LLM-specific tracing with evaluation attached, which is the seam into @sec-production-eval |

: Beyond this chapter {tbl-colwidths="[42,58]"}

## What to remember {#sec-observability-summary}

- **An agent trace is a distributed trace, with three differences.** The payload
  is text and dominates volume; cost is an attribute rather than an afterthought,
  because token counts convert to money and roll up; and failure is often not an
  error, so a span with `status=OK` can hold a confidently wrong answer or a run
  that hit its ceiling.

- **The GenAI conventions moved, and most of them are unstable.** They now live
  in `open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai`, split out of the main
  semantic-conventions repository, which still carries forwarding notices at the
  old paths. Of the marked items in the span document as counted for this
  chapter, **286 are `Development` against 22 `Stable`**, and at that snapshot
  the new repository had no tagged release. Use them — they are the only shared vocabulary — but pin the version
  and record the pin.

- **Span names are formulaic, not free text.** `{operation} {model}` for a model
  call, `execute_tool {tool.name}` for a tool call. Getting this right is what
  makes someone else's dashboard work on your traces.

- **Record the responded model as well as the requested one.** They diverge
  exactly when an alias silently resolves to a new version — @sec-gateway's
  problem — and two attributes turn an invisible dependency change into a
  visible one.

- **@sec-serving's measurements are standard metrics.**
  `gen_ai.server.time_to_first_token` and
  `gen_ai.server.time_per_output_token` are in the specification, so the
  prefill/decode split is a dashboard rather than a one-off experiment.

- **Estimate telemetry volume before you turn content recording on.** Measured
  here: **4.8 spans and 3,167 bytes per run**, of which **48.3% was prompt and
  completion text** — and that was on 301-token prompts. Holding the structure
  fixed and scaling the text to @sec-summarization's realistic 890 tokens gives
  6,163 bytes and **73.4% content**; at @sec-serving's 4,258-token contexts,
  **93.0%**. [Whether you log prompts is a four- to fourteen-fold decision
  about your monitoring bill.]{.hl}

- **Sampling content is a cost control and a privacy control at once.**
  Structure on every run, content on a small share and on every error. Redact
  before export, in a span processor, so it happens once rather than five times
  differently — and remember that telemetry inherits the same residency and
  retention obligations as the database it copies from.

- **Your own dimensions have to reach every span, not just the root.** Span
  attributes are not inherited, so user, team and feature written on the root
  never reach the model spans you group by. Copy them onto every span with a span
  processor, and keep anything identifying out of baggage, which travels on
  outbound calls. Environment goes on the Resource, the outcome on the root span.
  You cannot group by a dimension you did not record, and the number a budget
  review needs is cost per *resolved task*, not cost per session.

- **Tracing tells you what happened, not whether it was any good.** Quality,
  faithfulness and safety belong to the evaluation layer and attach to traces as
  scores. A dashboard full of green spans is entirely compatible with a product
  that is confidently wrong.
